notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: ductores opens the section and the sentence, so the Greek leaders are the first thing we hear. It puts the blame for the trick on the Greek commanders from the start.

notes.label: Delay
notes.body: annis is held to the end of the line, so the reader feels the weight of ten long years of war before the trick is revealed.

notes.label: Enjambement
notes.body: The horse is of such a size that its construction bursts over the line

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: secta and abiete are separated by intexunt, so the words weave around the verb. The word order mirrors the planks being woven together.

notes.label: Vivid present
notes.body: The present tense makes the Greeks' deceit happen before the reader's eyes, which makes it more vivid and alarming.

notes.label: Vivid present
notes.body: The present tense shows the rumour spreading as if it were happening now. It suggests how easily the lie took hold.

notes.label: Interwoven word order
notes.trans: chosen bodies of men picked by lot
notes.body: The words for the chosen men are interwoven (delecta virum sortiti corpora). The tangled order mirrors the soldiers packed tightly together inside the horse.

notes.label: Vivid present
notes.body: The present tense makes the scene immediate, as if the reader watches the soldiers being sealed inside.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: suggests the dark vastness of the hidden recesses in the horse.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: a ship building term

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Virgil’s favourite adjective

notes.label: Chiasmus
notes.body: The phrases for the inside of the horse are arranged around ingentis, so the language itself seems to enclose a hollow space. It stresses how vast and deep the horse's belly is.

notes.label: Pregnancy vocabulary
notes.body: uterus can mean womb, so the horse is pictured as pregnant with soldiers. The image is sinister: the horse will "give birth" to the men who destroy Troy.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: used as a collective for the soldiers

notes.label: Vivid present
notes.body: The present tense ends the description with the horse full of armed men, leaving the reader with a sense of threat.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: mainly a prose term

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: notissima stresses how well known Tenedos once was. This contrasts sharply with what it has become (line 23): a poor and unsafe bay.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: with negative force is a colloquial term promoted to epic by Virgil

notes.label: Pallas
notes.body: Pallas Athena, goddess of crafts and war, called Minerva by the Romans. She favoured the Greeks and helped them build the horse.

notes.label: Tenedos
notes.body: A small island a few miles off the coast near Troy, where the Greek fleet hid while pretending to sail home.

notes.label: Priam
notes.body: The king of Troy during the war, father of Hector and Paris.

Find the words that describe the horse as if it were a living creature. What is the effect?
Tenedos was once famous and rich. Why might Virgil stress what it has become?

context.body:
After ten years of war the Greeks still could not take Troy. With the help of Athena (Minerva to the Romans) they built a huge wooden horse, hid their best warriors inside it, and left it on the shore as if it were an offering to the goddess for a safe journey home. The rest of the fleet sailed only as far as the island of Tenedos and waited out of sight.

The story was famous long before Virgil: in Homer's Odyssey the bard Demodocus sings of it, and Odysseus remembers the long wait inside the horse. Virgil tells it from the Trojans' side, as a tale of deceit and disaster.
